paragraphs.text: Phones use radiofrequency signals; electrical power systems are a separate low-frequency exposure category. A technology name alone does not specify tissue dose, the signal used or the part of the body exposed. The source records identify the exposure each study actually considered. Call time is a behavior measure, not a direct measurement of absorbed dose. COSMOS uses call-time estimates, INTERPHONE relies on recalled use, and HERMES models brain dose. These approaches should remain distinct when interpreting their results. A complete comparison also identifies the task and the body region. A handset transmitting beside the head during a voice call is a different arrangement from a device carried while idle. The clinical studies use their reported calling categories; those categories cannot be read as calibrated measurements of energy absorbed by every participant.

Everyday phone use includes different positions and activities. The selected studies do not measure all of them in the same way: phone use, front-pocket carrying and modeled brain dose are different proxies. Neither carrying a device nor reporting frequent use tells us its precise transmission pattern or absorbed dose. That distinction matters when a headline changes the question from “people reporting this habit” to “radiation causes this outcome.” The first is an observed comparison; the second requires a causal interpretation that these proxies alone do not establish. This is why exposure history needs more than a screen-time total. A long period looking at a downloaded document does not describe the same radio activity as a call. For the cancer, cognition and reproductive comparisons below, retain the specific use question or operator metric that generated the study’s groups.

The exposure guidance linked here addresses radiofrequency fields; it is distinct from the low-frequency guidance used for electrical power systems. A reported biological response must also be described by what changed. Sleep-EEG features, isolated-cell assays and diagnosed tumours are different endpoints, rather than interchangeable measures of injury. Animal and cell studies can contribute to hazard and mechanistic questions. To apply them to people, the comparison must account for species or tissue, absorbed dose, exposure schedule and temperature control. Their presence in a research library does not turn them into human clinical evidence.

Phones and accessories can also contain permanent magnets. In a laboratory test, close positioning of an iPhone 12 activated the magnetic response of selected pacemaker and defibrillator demo generators. The response depended on position and stopped when the phone was removed. This is evidence about a particular static-magnet interaction with device operation. No implanted patients were studied, and the experiment does not estimate clinical event frequency or compatibility across later products.

An exposure-reduction claim and a demonstrated health benefit are different claims. To judge either, look for a measurement made under defined operating conditions and, separately, evidence about the health outcome being claimed. A useful distance test would keep the phone, network connection, task and measuring method identifiable while changing position. It would then describe the resulting exposure quantity. The separate health question requires relevant outcomes observed over an appropriate period; the physical change alone cannot specify how much a particular disease risk changes.

paragraphs.text: Read each comparison by its outcome, population and exposure window. A finding about one diagnosis does not establish a verdict for every health outcome. The table keeps human observations separate from animal and cell experiments; opening a row shows the source records and their limits. The recovered COSMOS sleep analysis followed adults using operator-recorded voice calling near baseline and later questionnaire sleep outcomes. Most outcomes did not show a consistent adverse pattern. An insomnia association in the highest ordinary call-time group weakened when the proxy accounted for network-related RF differences. This weakens a simple RF-specific explanation, but the observational contrasts do not establish a particular behavioral cause.

An evening exposure question needs an evening measurement. The Generation R and INMA analysis compared usual all-day modelled dose with sleep, then used daily evening diaries and wrist-based sleep estimates in a smaller Spanish group. These are overlapping analyses with different instruments and recall windows. The authors reported shorter sleep in the higher evening call-dose group, alongside broadly null all-day results after their correction procedure. Estimated dose still depended closely on calling time and assumptions about power, network and position. The study therefore adds a useful timing comparison while leaving RF causation, the exact effect and clinical importance unresolved.

Cordless calling was analysed separately from mobile calling in the ExPOSURE baseline study. Parents estimated weekly use, and the analysis compared categories defined by the sample’s call distribution. Selected cordless contrasts involved particular reaction-time or accuracy tasks; most comparisons did not show a statistically significant association. These were reported-call groups rather than measured brain-dose groups, and the tasks were not diagnoses of cognitive disease. The authors suggested that parents might know home cordless use better than mobile use elsewhere, but that suggestion does not validate every estimate. Keeping this distinction prevents handset-use associations from being transferred to a continuously operating base station.

A prospective pregnancy cohort can help separate remembered phone habits from later concerns about a child. In MoBa, mothers reported phone talking during pregnancy before the developmental follow-up. Some early language and motor screens were more favourable among phone users, while other screens showed no adjusted association. This does not make RF exposure a developmental treatment: talking frequency also differed with education, age, family circumstances and personality, and fetal dose was not measured. Some paternal comparisons pointed in the same direction. The useful finding is a bounded human comparison without an adverse signal in the selected screens, accompanied by a plausible social-confounding explanation that remains unproven.

Lower average birth weight and more low-birth-weight babies are different findings. The Kumamoto study reported the former among women classified as excessive phone users, but did not detect a significant difference in the clinical low-weight category. Its excessive-use classification came from a text-message dependency scale, and the reference group consisted of ordinary users. This makes the study relevant to phone-use behaviour during pregnancy, while leaving fetal RF dose unresolved. Social differences between the groups and unmeasured mental-health factors also matter. The result should therefore be described as a small observational association, without converting it into proof that phone radiation restricts fetal growth or a rule about safe daily use.

overview.text: Mobile-phone research is a collection of different comparisons. The cancer evidence included here contains prospective cohorts and the INTERPHONE case-control study. Their findings need to be read together: the cohorts did not show increased risk under their studied conditions, while INTERPHONE’s highest recalled-use group had elevated glioma odds. Recall, participation, exposure error and latency affect what those findings can establish.

paragraphs.text: The source description includes both the access point and the devices communicating with it. An antenna’s radiation pattern and the operating state affect what is measured at a particular location. A Wi-Fi label alone does not identify absorbed dose at the head or a room-average field. The recovered sleep exposure-facility paper describes an engineered head-exposure system, not a separate trial showing a health effect. Its dosimetry depends on position and geometry. That methods companion should remain attached to the experimental family rather than counted as independent replication. The distinction between router and client matters in practice: an access point can be across a room while a transmitting laptop is beside the user. Naming the network does not identify the source closest to the body. The measured operating state and traffic therefore belong with any reported field level.

An exposure schedule does not tell us how much radiofrequency energy reached the body. In the Shokri rat experiment, the authors named the antenna units, described the chamber and compared different daily exposure durations. They did not report their own measured field strength, power density, absorbed dose or data-traffic pattern. Rats could move within the setup, so positions relative to the antennas also varied. These details matter when interpreting the reported sperm and tissue findings: a device operating in a Wi-Fi band is not enough to establish that the rats received an exposure comparable to a person using a home router. The missing dose information limits translation of this experiment.

School measurement reports characterize transmissions from access points and laptops during particular applications. Their duty factors differ, and application traffic can alter airtime. These are exposure measurements, not trials of pupils’ sleep, fertility or development. A survey at multiple sites compared measured fields with public guidance under its stated conditions. Bystander measurements are not equivalent to contact exposure from a laptop. The tested distances and use patterns matter more than treating one maximum measurement as a universal home value. A survey of an occupied classroom and a maximum-output laboratory test can both be informative, while answering different questions. One describes a sampled activity and location; the other characterizes a specified operating condition. Neither becomes a continuous record of a child’s personal exposure simply because it concerns school equipment.

A school measurement can describe an operating network without being a child’s personal dose. The Australian survey used moving classroom checks and fixed-position samples, reporting both averages and recorded maxima. Active network traffic slightly raised the walkthrough average, while the peak comparison was not statistically significant. Intermittent transmissions help explain why those quantities differ. Most classrooms were empty, with limited observations in occupied rooms, so these samples do not describe every class size, task or traffic load. The study is useful for understanding measurement windows and source activity; it did not monitor individual sleep or other health outcomes.

paragraphs.text: Waking EEG and psychomotor vigilance did not change measurably in the recovered acute experiment’s abstract. That concerns awake participants and the specified tasks. It is not an overnight-sleep experiment or a long-term neurological disease study. The memory paper reported improved word-pair retention after Wi-Fi, with no significant difference in emotional or procedural memory. The authors classified the declarative result as inconclusive because associated physiology did not corroborate it and chance remained possible. It is not evidence that Wi-Fi improves learning. An EEG or memory result should retain its actual outcome and study window. A change in one physiological feature is not a diagnosis, and a failure to detect another feature is not proof that every possible effect is absent. The source’s full-text or abstract-only basis remains material to how closely its methods can be assessed.

paragraphs.text: A guideline comparison, an engineered exposure condition and a household average answer different questions. Compatible quantities and averaging are necessary before comparing them. The FOPH WLAN guidance is useful exposure context, rather than a substitute for outcome-specific clinical evidence. The sleep paper’s full text was not recovered in this run. Its abstract supplies the reported design and findings, but not a complete assessment of exclusions, allocation, analytic decisions or precision. The source record marks this limit instead of promoting an abstract into a completed full-text review. The averaging period and test arrangement determine what the number describes. A peak observed close to equipment cannot be substituted for a classroom average, and an external field reading is not automatically an absorbed brain dose. A health interpretation requires the outcome-specific evidence in addition to the applicable measurement comparison.

Position can change the field and absorbed-dose pattern. A directional exposure system designed for a sleeping volunteer does not reproduce every domestic router position. Home placement, device traffic and body geometry must be established before a quantitative comparison. Switching a router off changes transmission, but demonstrating a sleep benefit requires an intervention comparison that measures sleep and controls relevant alternatives. The recovered acute laboratory experiments do not establish that household intervention’s clinical benefit. For example, moving a router changes its contribution at a location while leaving any nearby client transmitter to be assessed separately. The relevant report should identify both ends of the connection and their activity. That makes an exposure claim testable without pretending that a distance choice has an already quantified clinical benefit.

Distance comparisons need the room geometry as well as a number. In the Australian school survey, the furthest desk generally had lower Wi-Fi readings than the nearest desk, while the position near the access point and the nearest desk were more similar. These were selected positions within existing rooms, containing different access-point placements and other transmitters. They do not establish a universal distance formula for every classroom or home. A useful comparison therefore records the source, sampling height, traffic and averaging period alongside distance. Nor does a lower external field reading by itself measure a change in sleep or symptoms.

The sleep and memory publications belong to one participant family; the facility report is methodological. Restricted healthy male samples and acute exposure limit generalization. The memory analysis is exploratory, with no correction for multiple testing and an exposure-order imbalance after exclusions. Seven Wi-Fi reports remain abstract-only in this recovery. The inspected memory full text is a publisher web snapshot; its original PDF and supplement were unavailable. Source checking supports these bounded statements, while systematic synthesis, scientific appraisal and human review remain pending. The most useful reading starts by separating exposure measurements, acute controlled experiments and longer observational comparisons. A school survey can improve the first category without adding a sleep or cancer result. A memory task cannot fill a missing sleep outcome. Where original methods remain unavailable, that access gap continues to limit appraisal.

In the ABCD sleep analysis, household Wi-Fi was represented by a parental report that the home had wireless internet when the child was younger. The comparison also separated homes with and without cordless phones. It did not record the router’s overnight operating pattern, the child’s distance from it or the energy absorbed during sleep. That makes this a comparison of household exposure indicators, rather than an experiment switching an otherwise identical router on and off. The broader findings varied across those indicators and phone-use reports. They can inform questions about measurement and confounding, but they cannot establish that a nighttime router change improves sleep or assign a precise sleep risk to a particular home network.

The published exchange about the Shokri rat experiment is useful context, but adds no second experiment. The critics questioned the exposure geometry, the absence of a sham group and the antenna description. In reply, Shokri described freely moving animals and changing cage positions, and stated that geometry was not measured. He defended the control choice, but did not supply a measured dose, field map or a new demonstration that conditions were equivalent between groups. These are attributed methodological positions rather than a formal correction or independent replication. They leave the original sperm and tissue findings to be assessed with the parent report’s exposure, control and reporting limitations.

The sleep abstract describes a blinded sham-controlled crossover in healthy young men. paragraphs.text: Electrical power systems are a low-frequency exposure category. The linked studies concern residential 50–60 Hz magnetic fields or wiring and distance proxies. A result about these exposures cannot be transferred to Wi-Fi merely by referring to both as EMF. The epidemiological question is usually about a person’s residential magnetic-field history, while a line’s presence is a description of infrastructure. Those variables are connected imperfectly. A useful report identifies whether its comparison used measurements, a reconstructed field, wiring characteristics or distance, rather than treating each as a direct measurement of the same quantity.

Residential exposure needs a time window and a way of measuring or estimating the field. A single appliance reading and a long-term residential category do not describe the same thing. Distance, wiring and field measurements can each capture different features of a setting. The studies linked here do not establish a complete exposure profile for a particular house. Reading their results requires keeping measured fields, estimated fields and distance-based categories separate. The timing of residence matters too. A birth address, a later home measurement and a residential history can represent different windows. They should not be silently substituted for one another when comparing studies. That distinction helps explain why an address-based analysis does not automatically describe the field in a child’s bedroom throughout childhood.

The epidemiological observation is an association, rather than a demonstrated biological mechanism. These selected human studies cannot by themselves establish the pathway from an external magnetic field to childhood leukaemia. The low-frequency guidance is a separate context source, not another independent cohort. The childhood-leukaemia association requires a causal explanation that fits the observed exposure and outcome, with alternatives assessed. Established physical interactions used in exposure guidance do not by themselves prove that explanation. Conversely, an unresolved mechanism is not a reason to erase an observed association; it is a limitation to retain when judging what the observations mean.

paragraphs.text: The meningioma report found no conclusive association with mobile or cordless use; its highest cumulative-use signal lacked a consistent latency pattern. The pooled acoustic-neuroma report found higher odds with longer wireless-phone histories. Retrospective histories, small long-latency groups and overlapping samples require appraisal before combining those findings. A base-station measurement cannot settle that disagreement. A longitudinal Australian child study measured cordless and mobile calling separately using parent reports. Children repeated several cognitive tasks, and the analysis compared changes in calling with changes in performance. An isolated cordless detection-accuracy finding occurred alongside many non-significant comparisons; mobile-task changes ran in different directions. Reported call counts, attrition and multiple tests limit causal interpretation. This is follow-up of the ExPOSURE programme, rather than an independent replication of its earlier cross-sectional report.

The QUALIFEX sleep report also collected cordless and mobile call duration separately from modelled ambient exposure. Some longitudinal contrasts were nominally significant, but the results did not form a consistent adverse exposure-response pattern across sleep outcomes and exposure measures. Call duration does not isolate absorbed RF from behaviour. The linked actigraphy subset belongs to the same cohort, and neither component randomly assigned cordless-phone use.

The ABCD report compared children’s recalled cordless calling with several parent-reported sleep scores. It did not show a consistent adverse cordless pattern, but the adjusted table contains isolated favorable waking and daytime-sleepiness contrasts, so describing every result as null would also oversimplify the source. These comparisons involved multiple related outcomes and did not measure a clinical benefit. They also concern reported calling, whereas the presence of a cordless system at home was recorded separately. Neither measure established the child’s continuous nighttime exposure to its base. This study therefore adds a specific child-sleep comparison while leaving unanswered whether a particular handset, base operating mode or bedroom arrangement changes objectively measured sleep.

The preadolescent sleep analysis grouped mobile and DECT calls together when estimating call-related brain dose. It therefore cannot identify a separate cordless-phone effect. The higher evening call-dose group had shorter wrist-estimated sleep in the authors’ analysis, but estimated dose closely followed the duration of calls. Reasons for calling, arousal and time displaced from sleep remain alternative explanations that this observational design could not separate. The model also used assumed power and device-position inputs rather than measuring each child’s absorbed dose. This comparison belongs with handset calling evidence; it does not test a household base station or whether turning a router off improves sleep.

Cordless calling was analysed separately from mobile calling in the ExPOSURE baseline study. Parents estimated weekly use, and the analysis compared categories defined by the sample’s call distribution. Selected cordless contrasts involved particular reaction-time or accuracy tasks; most comparisons did not show a statistically significant association. These were reported-call groups rather than measured brain-dose groups, and the tasks were not diagnoses of cognitive disease. The authors suggested that parents might know home cordless use better than mobile use elsewhere, but that suggestion does not validate every estimate. Keeping this distinction prevents handset-use associations from being transferred to a continuously operating base station.

overview.text: Cordless telephones communicate over a short radio link between the handset and a base. The handset can be held against the head during a call, while a base is usually elsewhere in the room. paragraphs.text: A computational anatomical model can estimate internal fields that cannot readily be measured in a living person. It relies on assumed tissue properties, source behaviour and geometry. It does not observe symptoms, pregnancy outcomes or cancer. The distinction is essential when a paper’s discussion moves from modelled guideline comparisons to a broad health reassurance. The modeled internal quantity answers how a specified external field interacts with a represented body. It is not an observed illness in a passenger. To connect that physical estimate with a clinical claim, the argument would also need a relevant endpoint, population and exposure history; those inputs cannot be supplied by the anatomical model itself.

The appropriate comparison depends on whether the reported quantity is an external magnetic field or an induced internal electric field, and on frequency and averaging. These should not be mixed into a single undifferentiated “radiation level.” Numeric percentages from the recovered charging model remain held because parts of the report are inconsistent; the qualitative scope can still be explained. The printed comparison also needs to be internally consistent. If a switching-frequency series, averaging equation or reference assignment is unclear, the affected numerical conclusion stays unresolved. A qualitative description of what was modeled or measured can still be useful, provided that it does not certify the equipment or imply a demonstrated health effect.

Fields were simulated at selected distances and postures in the specified installation. Those calculations illustrate how geometry matters within that model. They do not establish a universal clinical safe distance for all charger cabinets, cable layouts, power ratings or passengers. A real installation would need data appropriate to its actual sources and operating conditions. The modeled geometry must also resemble the arrangement being assessed: the charger, person, cable and operating conditions are all part of the scenario. A modeled decrease with separation is informative about that setup. It does not become a validated personal-risk curve, a chronic disease threshold or an implant-specific compatibility guarantee.

The investigators also calculated hours in bed from reported bed and wake times and reported no adjusted exposure association for that measure, although the detailed results were not shown. Neither measure was an overnight recording of sleep. This distinction helps explain why a questionnaire-domain association cannot simply be translated into shorter objectively measured sleep, diagnosed insomnia or a benefit from removing a household source.

paragraphs.text: The COSMOS sleep report adds a prospective adult comparison to the acute laboratory experiments. The insomnia indicator was not a complete clinical diagnosis, and selection, proxy exposure and unmeasured behavior remain limitations. The QUALIFEX sleep follow-up combines prospective questionnaires with a smaller linked actigraphy and bedroom-measurement study. Several longitudinal contrasts were nominally significant, without a consistent adverse exposure-response pattern; the authors did not apply formal multiplicity correction. Such alternatives need an appropriate study comparison; they should not be asserted as the cause of a result without evidence. Animal fertility experiments can test changes in sperm and testicular tissue without showing that an animal is unable to reproduce. Shokri and colleagues reported lower sperm concentration, normal morphology and total motility after exposure to their antenna setup, alongside more prominent testicular tissue and apoptosis-related changes in the longer-duration group. It therefore adds an animal reproductive signal that needs comparison with other studies, while leaving the size and even the existence of a human fertility effect unresolved.

Fertility evidence also includes magnetic fields in the intermediate-frequency range, which should be distinguished from phone and Wi-Fi radiofrequency exposure. They did not detect an adverse pattern in the count, morphology or weight measures, but found more non-progressive movement and fewer immotile sperm in the higher-field group. This mixed pattern does not establish general cognitive damage. Development and repeated testing can improve performance within both groups, so within-child improvement is distinct from the estimated difference between changes in phone use. The earlier and later reports from an existing cohort should also be kept in their family. A baseline association and a subsequent change analysis can add different information about the same programme, while not becoming two independent replications. The Australian ExPOSURE baseline paper illustrates why the study title and the actual analysis should be read together. Its parent project was prospective, but this publication compared reported calling and cognitive performance at baseline. Most comparisons were not statistically significant, with selected slower-response or lower-accuracy results and exploratory differences by gender. Numerous tests were examined without a multiplicity adjustment, and the authors considered chance. The later change analysis follows some of the same children, so the two publications should remain one cohort family. A prospective pregnancy cohort can help separate remembered phone habits from later concerns about a child. Some early language and motor screens were more favourable among phone users, while other screens showed no adjusted association. NTP judged the evidence for malignant heart schwannomas in exposed male rats clear, with variation by sex and tumour. Ramazzini reported an increase in male-rat heart schwannomas at its highest tested exposure. These are bounded findings; translating them into human risk requires additional reasoning.

topics.takeaway: The included experiments reported animal tumour signals under their exposure conditions. They do not provide a numerical cancer-risk estimate for a person using a phone.

modules.label: Measurement

paragraphs.text: DNA fragmentation, oxidative stress, motility and vitality are distinct cellular measurements. The sample consists of purified sperm outside the body. Neither the name “human sperm” nor the detection of an assay change makes this a trial of fertility outcomes in men. The assay must also retain its biological unit and timepoint. A measured DNA-related change can describe the exposed preparation without demonstrating a stable mutation, a clinical cancer or inability to conceive. Repeated images or cells from one sample provide technical detail rather than independent people. Interpretation should identify what the assay detects and what further causal steps remain untested.

modules.title: Define the outcome before comparing results

paragraphs.text: The comparisons below preserve the exposure and population of the original public records. Read each finding with its main limitation. An unassessed exposure is not a finding of no association; rows from different populations and endpoints do not form a pooled effect. The corrected isolated-sperm report contributes a model-specific positive result, rather than a universal DNA-damage conclusion. The original figure correction and replicate reporting remain attached to its interpretation. A broader synthesis would compare cell type, dose, thermal control, assay, repetition and reporting integrity across actual experiments, instead of counting all biomarker changes as equivalent clinical injuries.

A plausible mechanism and a measured mechanism are different parts of an explanation. This rat study measured sperm characteristics, testicular structure, TUNEL staining and caspase-related activity. The authors discussed oxidative stress and reduced testosterone as explanations, but did not measure those intermediates in their own experiment. TUNEL-positive germ cells and caspase activity help describe a cell-death response; they do not by themselves establish direct mutagenesis, explain every sperm finding or demonstrate infertility. Keeping those steps separate makes the study more useful: its observations can inform a biological hypothesis, while later experiments need to test the proposed intermediate steps and whether the changes affect reproductive success.

The location and timing of a DNA-related signal matter. In this study, selected stress markers in testis tissue did not change significantly, while mature sperm showed oxidative labelling and fragmentation findings. A mitochondrial oxidative probe increased at earlier exposure periods and later returned toward control values; a global probe did not follow the same pattern. These observations help define a biological hypothesis rather than a universal response to RF. They do not by themselves establish that mitochondria are the first direct target, exclude a thermal contribution or show inherited disease. More targeted experiments would need to test those causal steps and connect them to meaningful reproductive outcomes.

A negative cell experiment is informative when its exposure and methods are clear, but its scope still matters. Luceri and colleagues measured DNA-damage markers in isolated lymphocytes and gene expression in both lymphocytes and yeast. The final analyses did not support an exposure-related effect in those assays. Some initially highlighted gene changes disappeared under the final statistical methods, illustrating why a preliminary list should not replace the completed analysis. At the same time, pooled donor samples, limited independent replication and culture-setting differences restrict what the result can exclude. It does not directly measure disease risk or settle every possible response to ELF magnetic fields.

A positive comet-assay result is a finding about DNA-damage-related migration in the tested cells, rather than a cancer diagnosis. Mihai and colleagues reported increased comet measures and altered cell-cycle distributions after a particular pulsed ELF exposure in Vero cultures. They proposed oxidative and repair-related explanations, but did not directly measure the proposed reactive oxygen species. The small number of independent repeats, missing blinding and viability details, and unclear comparison between exposure schedules constrain interpretation. This report can inform a mechanistic discussion while leaving the size, reproducibility and relevance of any human health effect unresolved. Human scientific review remains pending.

The isolated preparation and experimental exposure differ from intact-body physiology and ordinary phone carrying. Those differences are limits on translation, rather than variables that can be ignored because a result is statistically significant. The exposure must reach the relevant cells under conditions represented by the experiment. An intact body changes that question; the name of a device or a shared frequency band does not establish the match. A statistically detectable assay difference remains worth investigating, with its preparation, uncertainty and incomplete connection to disease explicitly retained. These limits identify the missing links a replication should examine.

modules.label: Controlled studies

paragraphs.text: The cellular exposure is controlled, but it is not a human randomized trial. The correction and distinction between biological and technical replication remain essential to reading the experiment. No human clinical grade is assigned from this source. A useful verification starts with independent biological preparations, a comparable sham condition and a measurement appropriate to the endpoint. It also checks whether reported images and corrected figures support the stated comparison. Multiple technical observations can improve measurement within a sample without increasing the number of independently exposed donors or resolving the clinical translation.

A well-characterized cell experiment can narrow a mechanistic question without settling every health question about 5G. Haidar and colleagues used blinded chamber assignment, measured exposure and temperature control to compare a particular 5G signal with sham conditions. Their redox and UV-lesion-repair assays found no significant RF-related differences. The work therefore contributes useful negative laboratory evidence. Its established cell lines, specific chemical and UV challenges, and short exposure periods still limit generalization to intact skin or chronic exposure in people. Absence of statistical significance also does not establish that every possible small effect or DNA-repair pathway was excluded. Human scientific review remains pending.

modules.title: What controlled and sham studies can test

paragraphs.text: An exposure guideline and an outcome-specific health assessment are different documents. The original ICNIRP guideline and low-frequency information are linked as context; this selected-source edition does not assign an agency-wide verdict to each outcome. A document’s role, date and exact scope matter. IARC’s 2011 radiofrequency classification is historical cancer-hazard context. It should not be treated as a probability of harm for an individual or as a sleep, symptom or fertility assessment. No current multi-agency comparison is claimed here. A general exposure limit and a cancer classification do not determine the meaning of a particular DNA assay. The mechanistic argument needs the actual cell system, measured change and exposure conditions, plus evidence linking that change to a relevant disease endpoint.

modules.label: Interventions

paragraphs.text: The selected studies are not trials showing that a shielding product, sticker, fabric or change in device use improves this outcome. A laboratory attenuation result would answer an engineering question; demonstrating a health benefit requires an appropriate health-outcome comparison. Do not treat the presence of an association as proof that reversing an exposure improves health. Evaluate the exact claim being made: reduction in a measured field, reduction in actual user exposure, or a change in a clinical outcome. These claims need different evidence. No product-specific health recommendation follows from the selected records on this page.

modules.title: Evidence for interventions and product claims

overview.text: DNA-damage claims need to identify the cells, assay, exposure and correction status. The selected record here concerns purified human sperm outside the body, rather than an intact-person experiment. Its reported cellular changes are therefore a model-specific finding.

The study’s correction replaces Figure 1D and specifies biological replicates. Keeping that notice attached to the source matters more than repeating the title alone. A laboratory observation can inform a mechanism question without supplying a clinical diagnosis or a direct estimate of everyday risk.

topics.takeaway: The selected isolated-sperm experiment reported DNA fragmentation and other cellular changes. It does not establish disease or infertility from everyday exposure.

topics.intro: Infertility, miscarriage, preterm birth and fetal growth are different outcomes. Exposure proxies and timing are central to each comparison.

paragraphs.text: The Babol study compared clinic-defined infertility with controls, using residential proximity to power lines. The two-town pregnancy cohort followed miscarriage while recording fields at outdoor locations. The birth-cohort analysis studied gestational duration, fetal growth and birth weight, and the induction study used reported delivery information. These outcomes require different denominators and observation windows. The timing of the exposure information matters as much as the endpoint name. Recalled device use during a pregnancy differs from a prospectively recorded personal dose. A clinical group defined by a birth outcome also does not establish the direction of every associated behavior. The relevant comparison keeps gestational timing, selection and measurement separate from the authors’ proposed explanation.

The word development can hide important differences between outcomes. The MoBa report assessed a parent’s description of sentence structure, selected communication questions, and motor skills. It did not independently diagnose every child, and the motor questionnaire changed between follow-ups. Children not yet talking were excluded from the sentence comparison, so a reassuring result for that analysis cannot cover every severe language condition. The recovered supplement makes these choices visible by listing the actual questions and scoring. Reading those details explains why a study may inform selected preschool skills without settling every question about prenatal exposure, developmental disability or later childhood health.

modules.label: Evidence

paragraphs.text: Babol reported an infertility association with proximity. The miscarriage cohort differed by field metric: front-door averages were not predictive, while maximum alley values were associated. More frequent maternal calling was associated with shorter gestation in a four-cohort analysis, without a fetal-growth or birth-weight association. Some induction-use categories related weakly to preterm delivery, but the authors judged bias and other explanations important. The four-cohort pregnancy paper is another example of complementary information within established study families. It combines cohort-specific estimates rather than recruiting four new independent replications of every earlier birth-cohort report. The authors note that reported calling could reflect factors such as stress and that some information was collected well after pregnancy. The induction study has a different exposure proxy and its own follow-up and response problems. A reliable overview needs those differences beside the findings; it should not convert the presence of several papers into a single combined estimate of risk from any electrical device.

A retrospective Konya hospital study reported higher listed phone-model SAR among mothers of babies classified as small for gestational age, while recalled daily use-time was similar between growth groups. It assigned SAR from a phone listing rather than measuring maternal or fetal dose. Selection, recall, no reported adjusted causal model and a covariate-table inconsistency limit interpretation. The same-data prediction cutoff is not an independently validated safety threshold.

Lower average birth weight and more low-birth-weight babies are different findings. The Kumamoto study reported the former among women classified as excessive phone users, but did not detect a significant difference in the clinical low-weight category. Its excessive-use classification came from a text-message dependency scale, and the reference group consisted of ordinary users. This makes the study relevant to phone-use behaviour during pregnancy, while leaving fetal RF dose unresolved. Social differences between the groups and unmeasured mental-health factors also matter. The result should therefore be described as a small observational association, without converting it into proof that phone radiation restricts fetal growth or a rule about safe daily use.

modules.title: The recovered findings are not one pattern

modules.label: Confounding

paragraphs.text: Distance is not a personal field measurement. Outdoor readings without activity records do not describe every pregnancy’s dose. Phone-call frequency can reflect stress and other behaviours, and retrospective reporting adds uncertainty. Induction use and medical outcomes were self-reported in an internet panel. These issues affect causal interpretation even when a statistical association is present. For the cooker study, reported use is not the same as an absorbed maternal or fetal quantity. For the phone-model study, a published model rating does not measure an individual’s pregnancy exposure. These distinctions limit a dose-response interpretation and leave household, socioeconomic and other recorded or unrecorded differences to be considered in the causal appraisal.

A large-looking relative estimate can come from very few events. In this local pregnancy study, infant emergency transport was uncommon, the adjusted association was imprecise, and the authors acknowledged a chance explanation. Several newborn size and maternal variables were included in the model, but the report did not explain the transport indications or diagnoses. Statistical adjustment cannot manufacture information that a sparse dataset lacks. Before treating such a result as a clinical warning, readers need a stable, clearly defined outcome, an appropriate comparison and replication with enough events. Here, the finding raises a question for further study while leaving both its explanation and relevance to RF exposure unresolved.

modules.title: Exposure and confounding remain major limits

modules.label: Controlled studies

paragraphs.text: The induction-cooker measurement study helps estimate fields from cooking position and appliance features, but does not show a pregnancy effect. Its fixed-position estimates also require duration information and wider validation. Animal or isolated-cell results would answer separate mechanistic questions and cannot be substituted for human conception or birth outcomes without a justified translation. A controlled physical model can help answer how a specified source interacts with a represented body, while having no observed pregnancy outcome. An animal or cell experiment adds its own biological endpoints. Combining those sources requires an explicit match in exposure, relevant developmental timing and endpoint rather than assuming that one fills the clinical data missing from another.

modules.title: A measurement model is not an outcome trial

modules.label: Agency assessments

paragraphs.text: FOPH’s induction fact sheet distinguishes measured configurations and limit comparisons from the limited pregnancy literature. HSE’s workplace framework separately considers expectant workers at particular risk, within its UK remit. Neither document makes all home sources equivalent or supplies an individual prediction from one household reading. Formal source appraisal remains necessary for each outcome. The recovered RF reproductive protocol includes pregnancy and developmental outcomes in experimental mammals exposed in utero. That experimental stream is distinct from observational pregnancy studies in people. Its planned exposure controls and bias assessment describe how evidence would be assessed, rather than a completed conclusion about miscarriage, birth outcomes or human risk.

modules.title: Guidance and clinical outcomes have different scopes

modules.label: Interventions

paragraphs.text: These selected reports do not test an EMF product, avoidance programme or household distance rule as a way to improve conception or birth outcomes. Changing a source can alter a physical exposure while leaving the causal and clinical questions unresolved. A useful future study would measure exposure more directly, define outcomes prospectively and account for stress, socioeconomic circumstances and other environmental contributors. A claimed reproductive benefit needs the relevant clinical endpoint and timing. A reduction in a measured field does not show improved conception, gestational duration or birth outcome, and those outcomes cannot substitute for one another. A useful comparison would document the actual change, a suitable comparator and relevant differences between groups. The observational cooker and phone-model reports do not supply such a trial. Their signals and limitations can inform future questions without justifying a product claim or treating a derived exposure category as a preventive threshold.

modules.title: No reproductive treatment has been demonstrated

overview.text: This page separates the ability to conceive from outcomes after conception, including miscarriage, gestational duration and birth weight. It also separates phone calling, power-line proximity, residential magnetic-field readings and induction cooking. Those measures do not represent one common dose, even when reports are grouped under “EMF.”

The recovered full texts provide specific observations, with scientific review still pending. Repeated reports from the same clinic or cohort are not automatically independent confirmation. This remains selected-source coverage rather than a completed reproductive systematic review, and the present selection does not resolve every source or pregnancy outcome.

topics.takeaway: The recovered observational reports are mixed and use imperfect exposure measures. They do not establish a general reproductive effect or a proven EMF intervention.
